summary:
EarthScope (https://earthscope-chi.vercel.app) answers NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!”, making climate trends accessible and trustworthy. Users choose a location on a 3D globe, a period, and one of 13 variables. Live NASA POWER data yield trends per decade, 95% intervals, autocorrelation-corrected Mann–Kendall tests, five robustness checks, and minimum detectable trends. Increases or decreases are claimed only when supported by evidence. Native-cell maps control false discoveries; comparisons with another rainfall record and location cross-check results. An exploratory linear projection must beat the historical mean on held-out years.

In Puebla (2001–2024), temperature rose 0.45°C/decade (95% CI 0.23–0.70; p=0.009) and warm nights rose 5.5 percentage points/decade; both passed all checks. Tehuacán also warmed (0.62°C/decade). Tlaxcala rainfall records conflict (MERRA-2 +185 vs. GPM IMERG −27 mm/decade), so no rain trend is claimed.

For citizens, educators, planners, and researchers, EarthScope uses NASA POWER/MERRA-2 and GPM IMERG, plus NOAA stations for offline validation. AI tools assisted development, but no AI runs in the app or generates climate data; statistics are independently tested. Limitations include grid-cell versus station differences, a short 24-year record, and projections that are not forecasts. Future work: MODIS/VIIRS, multi-source comparisons, and broader station validation.
details:
EarthScope — NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

1. What does your project do, and how does it work?

We developed EarthScope, a free web application that allows anyone to explore long-term climate trends using NASA data for almost any location on Earth. Our goal is to make climate information easier to understand while providing the statistical evidence needed to evaluate how reliable each result is.

To use our application, users select a country or state on an interactive 3D globe, choose an analysis period (2001–2024 by default), and select one of 13 climate variables. These include mean, maximum, and minimum temperature; diurnal temperature range; the hottest day and coldest night of the year; warm days and warm nights; annual and wet-season precipitation; specific and relative humidity; and root-zone soil wetness.

Once users click Analyze, our server retrieves the corresponding data directly from the NASA POWER API using MERRA-2, without requiring accounts or API keys.

Before analyzing the data, we remove missing and physically implausible values. We also require all 12 months of a year to contain valid observations before including that year in the analysis. From these observations, we construct annual and seasonal time series and calculate anomalies relative to the 1991–2020 reference period.

To determine whether a climate variable is changing, we calculate its trend per decade, a 95% confidence interval, and a Mann–Kendall test with the Hamed–Rao correction for temporal autocorrelation. We also apply Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate control across the 13 variables, five predefined robustness checks, and an estimate of the minimum detectable trend.

We classify the evidence as robust, probable, weak, or not detectable. This classification determines how we communicate the results. For example, we only describe a variable as increasing or decreasing when the statistical evidence supports that conclusion.

We also integrated additional features to help users explore and verify their results:

  • Spatial analysis: We display native NASA POWER grid cells on a map, including field-wide statistical significance control.
  • Independent comparisons: We compare precipitation results with GPM IMERG, a second NASA rainfall record, and allow users to repeat an analysis at another location.
  • Exploratory projections: We generate linear projections only when they outperform the historical mean on held-out years.
  • Local impact indicators: We include water and heat impact lenses for Mexican municipalities.
  • Reproducibility: We provide an evidence file containing the exact NASA data request used in each analysis.

Finally, we allow users to share their results through a direct link.

2. What benefits does it have?

When developing EarthScope, we wanted to address several problems that make climate information difficult to access, interpret, and trust.

First, we made the application accessible to everyone. Users do not need an account, technical knowledge, or specialized software. They can select a location and obtain an analysis with an understandable explanation of the results.

Second, we focused on statistical reliability. Climate records contain natural variability, and a visible change does not necessarily indicate a statistically supported trend. To address this, we implemented autocorrelation-corrected statistical tests, multiple-testing control, and predefined robustness checks.

We also wanted to avoid a common misunderstanding: when a trend is not statistically detected, that does not necessarily mean the climate has remained unchanged. Instead of reporting "no change," we show the minimum detectable trend so users can understand the limitations of the available data.

Another important benefit is transparency. We allow users to trace each result to the exact NASA request, and we developed automated tests that reproduce our calculations using real NASA responses.

We also pay attention to spatial accuracy. The observations we analyze represent a 0.5° × 0.625° grid cell, not a measurement taken directly in a city or at a weather station. We clearly communicate this distinction and display the cell's mean elevation.

Additionally, we integrated independent comparisons to identify disagreements between datasets. For example, in Tlaxcala, MERRA-2 suggests a precipitation increase of +185 mm per decade, while GPM IMERG indicates −27 mm per decade. Because these records disagree, we do not make a precipitation trend claim.

Finally, EarthScope has nearly global coverage, allowing users to investigate climate trends across countries and regions using the same analytical methodology.

3. What is the intended impact?

With EarthScope, we want to make NASA climate data useful at a local level without exaggerating what the observations can demonstrate.

We designed our application for different types of users. Students and citizens can investigate how climate conditions have changed in their regions while learning to distinguish meaningful trends from statistical uncertainty.

Teachers and science communicators can use EarthScope to explain climate trends through interactive visualizations and share reproducible analyses rather than static images.

We also believe the application can be useful for local planners and agricultural extension workers, particularly in regions where meteorological stations are limited. Our platform provides access to consistent historical records while clearly communicating their limitations.

For researchers, we offer a way to perform an initial climate assessment, review the statistical methodology, and access the corresponding NASA data requests.

One example of what we achieved is our analysis of Puebla, Mexico, for 2001–2024. We identified an increase in mean air temperature of +0.45 °C per decade, and the result passed all five robustness checks.

In the long term, we would like EarthScope to become a useful resource in classrooms, science communication activities, and local planning discussions. More importantly, we hope our project demonstrates how open Earth observation data can be communicated responsibly, making scientific information understandable without sacrificing accuracy.

4. What tools did you use?

To develop EarthScope, we combined NASA Earth observation datasets, modern web development technologies, statistical analysis tools, and automated testing.

Data sources

Our main source of climate information is the NASA POWER API v2.10, which provides access to MERRA-2 data and GPM IMERG precipitation records through POWER.

We also used the following sources:

  • NOAA GHCN-Daily: We used ground-based weather station records to validate our results.
  • CONAGUA/SMN: We consulted meteorological station records and the Mexican Drought Monitor.
  • INEGI: We used the 2020 Census and the 2020 Geostatistical Framework for geographic and demographic context.
  • Natural Earth: We used geographic boundaries for our maps.
  • NASA Blue Marble: We integrated satellite imagery to visualize Earth on our interactive globe.

Programming languages

We developed the application using TypeScript, CSS, and Bash. We also used Python 3, relying exclusively on its standard library, to perform data audits and independently verify our statistical calculations.

Frameworks and libraries

For our web application, we used:

  • Next.js 16 and React 19.
  • three.js, react-globe.gl, and three-globe for the interactive 3D visualization.
  • SWR for data fetching.
  • Tailwind CSS 4 for styling.
  • shadcn/ui with Base UI for interface components.
  • Lucide for icons.

Testing and code quality

We used Vitest, ESLint, and TypeScript to test our implementation, detect errors, and maintain code quality.

Deployment and development workflow

We used Vercel to deploy EarthScope, along with Docker, pnpm, Git, and GitHub for development, dependency management, and collaboration.

Our application is available at:

https://earthscope-chi.vercel.app

Demonstration video and documentation

For our demonstration video and technical report, we used HyperFrames, GSAP, FFmpeg, Playwright, and LaTeX.

Artificial intelligence assistance

During development, we used Claude Code (Anthropic), Gemini (Google), and Codex (OpenAI) as programming assistants.

These tools helped us with development tasks, but our team reviewed, evaluated, and tested their contributions.

We want to emphasize that EarthScope does not use AI models to analyze climate data or generate conclusions. All calculations are performed using our implemented statistical methods, and no climate data or media were generated by AI.

5. How is your project creative?

We believe EarthScope's main innovation is not simply displaying climate data, but changing how users interpret and evaluate climate trends.

Most climate visualization tools focus on showing changes through graphs, maps, or colored indicators. We wanted to go further by making statistical evidence a central part of the user experience.

One of our main design principles is that every trend claim must be supported by evidence. We do not automatically display an increasing or decreasing trend simply because a line slopes upward or downward. The statistical results determine which conclusions the application can communicate.

Another feature we consider important is showing what the available data cannot tell us. Instead of interpreting a nonsignificant result as evidence that nothing has changed, we calculate the minimum detectable trend. This helps users understand the limits of their analysis.

We also implemented a comparison between two NASA precipitation records, MERRA-2 and GPM IMERG. Both datasets are evaluated under predefined rules, and disagreements can prevent the application from issuing a trend claim.

Our exploratory projections follow a similar principle. We only display a projection when it performs better than the historical mean on held-out years. We also include a 95% prediction interval and explicitly label the result as "exploratory, not a forecast."

Finally, we designed our spatial visualization to respect the original resolution of the data. Our maps display native grid cells without smoothing, avoiding the impression that the information is more geographically precise than it actually is.

Through these decisions, we wanted to create a platform that encourages users to question, understand, and verify climate information rather than simply accept a visualization.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Throughout the development of EarthScope, we made several decisions to ensure that our application would be scientifically responsible, accessible, and useful.

Scientific integrity

One of our main priorities was avoiding misleading statistical conclusions.

We considered temporal autocorrelation, multiple hypothesis testing, and the relatively short length of our climate time series.

We defined our evaluation thresholds before examining the results and assessed their behavior through sensitivity analyses. We did not adjust these thresholds afterward to obtain more favorable conclusions.

We also verified our statistical calculations using an independent Python reference implementation.

Data quality and validation

Before selecting the variables included in EarthScope, we audited NASA POWER data and evaluated their suitability for our analysis.

From the variables we examined, we retained 13 and excluded 17 based on the results of our audit.

We also compared NASA POWER data against meteorological station observations. During this process, we found that POWER precipitation records poorly reproduced year-to-year rainfall variations. For this reason, we decided not to issue precipitation trend claims.

Another important consideration was the handling of incomplete observations. We represent missing years as gaps rather than zeros to avoid introducing artificial changes into the time series.

We also included a warning about the 2014 transition from TRMM to GPM in the IMERG record, since this change may affect the interpretation of precipitation data.

Open access

We wanted anyone to be able to use EarthScope without encountering registration or authentication barriers.

For this reason, we selected publicly accessible data sources that do not require user accounts or API keys.

We also excluded data portals requiring NASA Earthdata authentication so that users, including competition judges, can run and evaluate our application without additional steps.

Honest handling of failures

We chose not to use simulated or fabricated climate data when a request fails.

If NASA POWER is unavailable or returns an error, our application informs the user and provides a retry option.

We believe it is better to communicate that data could not be retrieved than to display information that could be mistaken for real observations.

Responsible scientific communication

We designed EarthScope to identify and communicate statistical patterns, not to make unsupported claims about their causes.

We also distinguish exploratory projections from forecasts and avoid presenting our results as predictions of future climate conditions.

Similarly, our water and heat impact lenses provide contextual information without offering operational, agricultural, or medical instructions.

Usability and accessibility

Finally, we considered how people without technical or scientific backgrounds would interact with our application.

We designed the interface to present a clear, understandable summary first, while allowing users to explore the statistical evidence in greater detail.

We also incorporated accessibility considerations, such as respecting reduced-motion preferences and allowing projection animations to pause.

Our objective was to make EarthScope understandable to a general audience while preserving the technical depth needed for users who want to evaluate the underlying evidence.
